docs.title: FactHarborDSS
docs.text: Decision Support System · In planning

docs.title: Evidence for better-informed decisions
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is a planned tool for checking factual claims and, later, comparing courses of action. It aims to make conclusions easier to inspect and challenge—with clear evidence, reasons and uncertainty.

Designed for people and, later, working AI agents.

How it would work Cooperate with us

docs.title: Building on existing work
docs.text:
The project builds on lessons from the FactHarbor application (Alpha)—see its report walkthrough—and Evidence-Gated Agents: examine what supports a conclusion, and keep permission to share or act separate.

It is developed within the FactHarbor association, a Swiss non-profit.

docs.title: Where we are now
docs.text:
Planning stage — 28 October 2026. The first development phase would check public-web claims and preserve the evidence examined. Implementation has not started; DSS benefits have yet to be demonstrated.

Explore the planned architecture, why a fresh implementation, or partnership and funding opportunities.

docs.title: Planned architecture
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is in planning. The diagram shows the selected design, not an implemented or validated system.

Open the diagram for a larger view. Components show responsibilities, not security isolation. Original diagram; repository-wide licensing remains undecided.

docs.title: Core design
docs.text:
• One application: a TypeScript interface served by C#/.NET 10, with a worker initially running in the same process.
  • Traceable evidence: PostgreSQL stores captured web content, source versions, assessments, reports and durable jobs. Full-text search provides the retrieval baseline.
  • Repeatable evidence basis: reassessment uses the saved version without hidden fetching. Refreshes create new versions; model outputs may still differ.
  • Separate source evaluation: Source Reliability has its own service interface and database. Its role in the first milestone remains undecided.
  • Permissions enforced in code: access, report release and external actions are checked separately. Retrieved documents and AI assessments cannot grant authority; source restrictions also apply to derived reports.

The first milestone focuses on web evidence and minimal claim assessment. Broader decision workflows, working-agent access and controlled external actions come later. The pipeline explains the broader assessment and agent-debate design.

docs.title: Planning documents
docs.text: This repository's project concept and analysis pipeline complement this architecture overview. Agreed contributions need concrete requirements and acceptance criteria supplied alongside their scope.

docs.title: Association and projects
docs.text:
The FactHarbor association is a Swiss non-profit association (Verein), founded in 2026 and based in Dietlikon, Zürich. Its purpose is to help people make well-grounded decisions and use technology responsibly. Public benefit, openness, independence and transparency guide the work. Public stewardship overview

The association brings together two complementary initiatives. Its FactHarbor initiative develops applications and services for evidence-based decisions, including the existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) and the planned FactHarborDSS. Our AI Charter proposes a trustworthy AI network for free, fair and resilient societies. FactHarborDSS is planned to succeed both the FactHarbor application and the relevant Evidence-Gated Agents core, for claim assessment and decision support.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
These are different projects and maturity levels, not interchangeable names for a delivered system. The overview reflects the project presentation and the DSS planning status as of 28 October 2026.

Work What exists Intended contribution to DSS FactHarbor application (Alpha) An existing claim-checking application with evidence, sources, reasoning, truth assessment and separate confidence. Experience with claim assessment, report structure and the reader's inspection path. Our AI Charter Public framework, commitments, research and articles in draft form; a proposed network. Accountability, openness, traceability and the public-interest context. Evidence-Gated Agents A defined concept and prototype direction; DSS integration remains development work. Examine a proposed step's evidence and authority before permitted release or action. AI Charter Runtime A separate runnable but unfinished proof of concept, exercised with simulated scenarios and local effects. Lessons about controls outside the acting AI. Code reuse remains an explicit choice. FactHarborDSS Published concept, pipeline and architecture overviews; planning continues. A shared core for human and agent claim assessment and decision support. Not yet implemented or evaluated.

The Alpha's reports are concrete examples of an existing application. Charter documents describe principles and proposed structures. The Runtime proof of concept does not establish completed EGA integration, operational certification or DSS security.

The project concept and planned architecture in this repository describe the DSS direction.

docs.title: Continuity without assumed parity
docs.text:
DSS is intended to succeed the FactHarbor application and the relevant EGA core. That does not promise delivered feature parity, a replacement date, migration of all historical data or retirement of either predecessor. The FactHarbor association remains the organization behind this work.

Useful experience, report ideas and carefully selected work should carry forward. Implementation reuse needs case-by-case review. The initial DSS milestone acquires new web evidence; it does not depend on importing the Alpha's evidence or results.

Read what DSS would carry forward, Our AI Charter and EGA, and why a fresh implementation is proposed.

docs.title: Our AI Charter and Evidence-Gated Agents
docs.text: Our AI Charter is a public initiative proposing a trustworthy AI network for free, fair and resilient societies. It supplies the wider accountability context for the DSS direction. Its network and assurance structures remain proposals; they are not operational services or certification claims.

docs.title: Five connected pillars
docs.text:
The Charter organizes its work around five pillars:

  1. Accountable AI decisions and actions — evidence, authority and inspectable outcomes for consequential steps. Evidence-Gated Agents is the current focus within this pillar.
  2. Open, plural models — meaningful choice across models, languages and regions.
  3. Data and provenance commons — documented sources, rights, restrictions and access conditions.
  4. Shared assurance and evaluation — independent examination, review, correction and remedy.
  5. Federated public AI infrastructure — independently operated capacity connected through shared rules.

Read the Charter's five-pillar overview. The pillars describe complementary responsibilities, rather than capabilities already implemented in DSS.

docs.title: What an EGA check would do
docs.text:
A working AI proposes an exact next step. The EGA concept examines the evidence for that step, its authority and the applicable access, processing and disclosure permissions. A permitted step proceeds within its checked scope; otherwise it remains stopped with a recorded reason. Authorized human judgment is involved where needed.

Illustration by Robert Schaub and contributors, reproduced unchanged under CC BY-SA 4.0. Original illustration · Source licensing. Open the image for a larger view.

Evidence alone grants no permission. A recommendation, permission to disclose that recommendation and authority to execute an external action are separate. Revisions require a new check where applicable; uncertainty about whether an action occurred requires reconciliation, not automatic repetition.

docs.title: What exists and what remains
docs.text:
The public EGA work defines the concept and prototype direction. The separate AI Charter Runtime is runnable but unfinished, with simulated scenarios and local test effects. Neither establishes a completed DSS integration.

DSS is intended to provide a shared evidence and assessment core for humans and working AI agents. Its first development milestone is narrower: human-facing web evidence capture/replay and minimal claim assessment. Working-agent access and action integration remain later scope; see the planned architecture.

Explore EGA · Runtime proof of concept · Published articles

docs.title: What FactHarborDSS would do
docs.text:
FactHarborDSS is intended to turn a question into a conclusion whose evidence and reasoning people can inspect.

Use The question it helps answer Check a factual claim What supports or contradicts this claim, and how confident can we be in the assessment? Compare options — later Which course of action is justified by the evidence, given the person's confirmed goals and constraints?

docs.title: From question to an inspectable report
docs.text:
Broader planned approach, not delivered functionality. Additional-agent debate and decision comparison are later scope. Full pipeline and agent roles.

Simplified adaptation of the FactHarbor/DSS design. Attribution: FactHarbor contributors · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Public visual lineage.

docs.title: What the reader should gain
docs.text:
• An inspectable basis: the sources and passages actually examined.
  • A reasoned assessment: supporting evidence, objections and unresolved gaps.
  • An honest result: clear scope, uncertainty and limitations—including when no conclusion is justified.

For decisions, people set the priorities. A recommendation does not itself authorize sharing information or taking action.

docs.title: Start small, demonstrate usefulness
docs.text:
The first phase focuses on public-web claims and saved evidence that can be reassessed. Comparative evaluation would follow; file-based decision support comes later. DSS must demonstrate benefit against existing tools and workflows.

See the planned architecture or ways to cooperate.

docs.title: Partnerships and funded development
docs.text:
Help turn the planned FactHarborDSS into a useful tool through practical cases and independent evaluation, or funding and engineering capacity. The FactHarbor association provides the non-profit setting; the existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) offers reports to learn from.

DSS implementation has not started. The first phase would assess public-web claims and preserve the evidence examined. Comparative evaluation follows separately; file-based decision support comes later.

docs.title: Practical cooperation
docs.text:
For the first phase, contribute precise factual claims, public sources, independent evidence judgments, or readers willing to assess whether reports are useful. No private file collection is needed.

A later pilot would test one recurring type of decision against agreed goals and constraints, using permitted files and representative cases. Its scope and intended use still need to be selected.

Evaluation should examine evidence gaps, justified conclusions, reader effort, time and cost. These are questions to test, not promised improvements.

docs.title: Funded development
docs.text:
Funding and engineering capacity could support an initial phase with agreed deliverables:

  • Capture web evidence, preserve it for reassessment, and produce a minimal claim assessment.
  • Check traceability and the reader's ability to inspect sources and reasoning.
  • Report results, limitations and effort to inform the next decision.

Comparative assessment-quality evaluation and the later decision pilot need their own scope and resources. Successful development checks alone do not establish suitability for operational use.

This repository publishes the concept, pipeline and architecture overview. Detailed task requirements and acceptance criteria must be supplied before dependent work begins.

Partner introductions, research collaboration, fundraising and clear public communication are also welcome.

docs.title: Start a conversation
docs.text:
Describe the need, who would benefit, and the expertise or resources you could contribute. Use the contact routes, or open a public proposal following the contribution guide.

Agree scope, success criteria, budget, responsibilities and data permissions before work starts. Keep private evidence and protected evaluation cases or answers out of public messages. Cooperation does not itself authorize processing, publication, deployment or external actions.

No funding target, partner commitment or delivery date is established. Repository-wide licensing and any future application release remain undecided.

docs.title: From FactHarbor to DSS
docs.text: The existing FactHarbor application (Alpha) provides experience to build on. See the FactHarbor report walkthrough, including sources, evidence and separate assessment and confidence labels.

docs.title: What DSS would carry forward
docs.text:
DSS would retain inspectable claims, evidence, sources and limitations, keeping the assessment of a claim distinct from confidence in it. It would add a more explicit basis for preserving and replaying the evidence used, and later compare options against human-confirmed goals and constraints.

These are design intentions, not delivered capabilities or inherited proof of quality. DSS must demonstrate its own usefulness. The FactHarbor association remains the organization behind both applications.

See the purpose and approach, reasons for a fresh implementation and planned architecture.

docs.title: Analysis pipeline and agent debate
docs.text:
The planned pipeline connects an exact question to permitted evidence, an assessment people can challenge, and a report released to its intended reader. Claim assessment and decision comparison share evidence and reporting, while using distinct analytical methods.

This is the broader proposed design, not an implemented workflow. The first milestone remains web evidence capture/replay and minimal claim assessment. Decision comparison and the additional-agent debate route are later scope, subject to evaluation. More agents are not themselves evidence of better results.

Open the diagram for a larger view. The “Conditional agent debate” panel contains possible debate tasks; it does not prescribe all roles, parallel dispatch or a fixed number of model calls. The Validator role is represented in step 4 alongside trusted code checks; required validation applies on both routes.

Simplified adaptation of the FactHarbor/DSS design. Attribution: FactHarbor contributors · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Public visual lineage.

docs.title: What the agents would contribute
docs.text:
The controller selects only required or justified tasks, their dependencies and their permitted inputs. Each task works against the exact evidence and assessment versions it was assigned.

Task Contribution Advocate Explain the evidence-backed case, including assumptions and limitations; do not defend a preferred answer regardless of evidence. Challenger / specialist Examine counterevidence, alternative explanations, citation or scope defects, or a specific expert question. Self-consistency Examine instability or contradictions on comparable inputs. Repetition and agreement add no independent evidence. Reconciler Accept, reject or retain each material objection as unresolved, with reasons; revise affected findings where justified. Validator Apply the required qualified semantic checks, including whether citations support the claim. Trusted code separately checks reference existence, exact quotations, evidence dates, versions, arithmetic and current authority. It applies no source weights or evidence-count formulas. Validation grants no release or action permission.

These are task roles, not necessarily five permanent agents or five different models. Different role names do not establish independence. The controller joins only the dependencies it admitted, rejects stale or incompatible results, and retains an explicit outcome for failed or cancelled tasks.

docs.title: Challenge without voting or endless retries
docs.text:
Baseline assessment already examines counterevidence. When no extra agent is needed, the direct path still undergoes mandatory checks. A required challenge cannot be skipped because another agent agrees or the budget has run out.

Reconciliation follows the substance of an objection, not the number of agents supporting it. A demonstrated reasoning or quotation defect can justify correction without a new source; unsupported disagreement does not automatically reduce a score. Material unresolved issues constrain the conclusion and its intended use.

The controller can admit useful refinement or request human input within the same remaining resource allowance, or record a limited result, hold or stop. Further rounds do not reset limits. Deliberate scope narrowing or changed decision priorities require the applicable human adoption; a claim-only request needs no irrelevant preference approval.

docs.title: Judgment reliability
docs.text:
In the planned design, assessments rely on guided model judgment rather than hand-set weights. Reliability comes from recording, separating and measuring judgments:

  • Recorded basis: each assessment records the interpretation of the question or claim, the key details considered, the evidence capture dates, and the versions of the assessment schema and scale.
  • Separate states: conflicting evidence, insufficient evidence and no assessment are distinct outcomes.
  • Repeated runs: if runs are repeated on the same captured evidence, the verdict is never set by picking a favorable run, rerunning until runs agree, or voting or averaging. A single run means stability is not measured. Whether and how run variation is shown is decided after reader testing.
  • Separate measures: evidence sufficiency and any observed run variation stay separate and are never merged into one score. Run variation is also kept apart from the verdict and its confidence. A model's self-reported confidence is never used alone.
  • Source information, not source weights: source type, ownership, independence and track record inform the assessment and are shown to readers. They are never applied as a weight or gate. Publisher ratings recalled by a model are not used.

docs.title: From candidate to permitted report
docs.text:
Reports retain material objections, dispositions, changes, reasons, uncertainty and stopping conditions—not raw debate transcripts. Only a valid candidate becomes a fixed report edition. Recipient-specific access, disclosure, quality and any required human review still govern release; a misleading redaction must be withheld.

A report is evidence, not permission to act. External actions have a separate authorization and execution path and are outside this simplified diagram.

See the system architecture and purpose and approach.

docs.title: Why a fresh implementation
docs.text:
The proposed fresh implementation is intended to carry forward the experience and useful work from developing the FactHarbor application while creating a simpler foundation for claim assessment, later decision support and EGA. It starts with a small implementation whose benefits must be verified before the scope expands.

These are development motivations and intended improvements, not measured DSS results. A rewrite alone would establish neither better assessments nor market demand.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
The maintainer's experience is that the Alpha has accumulated considerable code and complexity, making changes harder to manage. A fresh modular structure is intended to make responsibilities clearer, reduce unnecessary coupling and make changes easier to review.

This does not imply discarding everything learned or automatically copying existing code. Useful designs and selected implementation candidates need deliberate reuse decisions.

docs.title: Speed and running costs
docs.text:
The intention is to simplify the analysis workflow and avoid unnecessary processing while protecting quality. More steps, agents or model calls are not a measure of better reasoning.

Any improvement must be demonstrated against a suitable baseline, considering assessment quality alongside time, cost and the reader's correction effort. No DSS speedup or cost saving has been established.

docs.title: Quality and testing
docs.text:
Preserving the exact evidence used by each assessment should make comparisons more systematic and regressions easier to detect. The design separates acquisition quality, assessment quality on fixed evidence and the usefulness of the complete reviewer workflow.

Repeatable inputs support investigation; they do not guarantee identical model output or correct conclusions. Independently judged cases, protected evaluation material and explicit acceptance criteria remain necessary.

docs.title: A common foundation for broader capabilities
docs.text:
Fact-checking asks what the evidence supports. Decision support adds human-confirmed goals, alternatives and constraints. EGA also asks whether a proposed step is supported and permitted to proceed.

These uses can share evidence and reporting while keeping their methods and authority boundaries distinct. See the concept for their purpose and the architecture for the selected foundations.

docs.title: Production readiness
docs.text:
The planned architecture is intended to improve the foundation for database storage, background processing, recovery and access controls, with a path toward more users and workloads. Durable work and explicit permissions should be designed into the application rather than assumed from an AI response.

This is a design direction, not production readiness already achieved. Capacity, recovery, access controls and hosting must be implemented and qualified for their intended use. See the architecture overview.

docs.title: Development with coding agents
docs.text:
Clear requirements, smaller modules, explicit interfaces and focused tests should make delegated changes easier to review and integrate. An accountable integrator, independent review where required and evidence-based acceptance remain necessary.

A better structure may help both human contributors and coding agents. It does not prove faster development, reliable autonomous operation or installed technical enforcement. The contribution guide explains how to propose scoped work.

docs.title: Start small and test the reasons
docs.text:
The first development target is bounded web evidence capture and replay with minimal claim assessment. Comparative evaluation follows separately. Continue, narrow or reconsider the work based on demonstrated benefit, not the fact that a rewrite has begun.

The initial work must therefore produce evidence about quality, usefulness and effort as well as functioning software. The cooperation options explain how cases, reviewers, engineering capacity and funding could support that process.
